opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it starts from a pretty simple observation: the biggest bottleneck in robot learning right now is data. In language and vision we had the internet, billions of examples people produced just by living their lives. Robotics doesn't have that. The dominant way we collect robot data today is teleoperation, where a person puppeteers a robot to do a task. It works, and it's given us some really impressive results, but it's slow and expensive, and it's fundamentally tied to having a physical robot in front of you. You can't scale it the way the internet scaled.

Humans, on the other hand, are doing manipulation all the time. Every time you cook, fold laundry, or open a drawer, you're generating exactly the kind of data a robot would need: how hands approach objects, how you grasp, how you recover when something slips, how you sequence a long task. If we can capture that from the first-person view, with something like smart glasses or a lightweight head-mounted camera plus hand tracking, then suddenly the data collection isn't bottlenecked by robots anymore. It's bottlenecked by people wearing a device, and that scales much more like the internet did.

The egocentric part matters a lot. Third-person video, like YouTube, is abundant, but the viewpoint, the embodiment, and the actions are all very far from what a robot actually experiences. First-person data is much closer. The camera sits roughly where a robot's head camera would be, you see the hands interacting with objects up close, and you can recover actual 3D hand motion. That makes the gap between the human and the robot something you can actually bridge, rather than something you have to hand-wave over.

Of course there's still an embodiment gap. Human hands aren't robot grippers, our kinematics are different, and the visual appearance is different. A big part of our research has been figuring out how to close that gap. You align the sensing so humans and robots see the world similarly, you align action spaces at a level both can share, like end-effector or hand pose trajectories, and you co-train on a large amount of human data together with a smaller amount of robot data. What we've found is that the human data isn't just a nice add-on. It meaningfully improves performance and generalization, especially to new scenes and objects the robot never saw in its own data.

So when I say human data could get us toward human-level robots, I mean that humans are the only existing example of human-level manipulation, and they're generating a huge stream of demonstrations of it every day. If we can learn to tap into that stream, robotics gets its own version of internet-scale data, and I think that's what will unlock the kind of generality we've seen in other areas of AI. It won't be the only ingredient. You still need robot data, reinforcement learning, and good hardware. But I think it's the ingredient that lets you scale.

r001.rationale: The response compares robotics data scaling to internet-scale data in language and vision, but it does not clearly state the analogy that human data enabled LLMs and could enable human-level robots.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I actually want to push back a little on the framing, because I don't think human data alone gets you to a human-level robot. But I do think it's one of the few scalable sources of the thing we're most starved for, which is diverse, long-horizon, physically grounded demonstrations of how to actually do stuff.

If you look at where the big breakthroughs in language and vision came from, it was essentially the internet giving us billions of examples of what humans produce. Robotics never had that. Every demonstration we collect with a robot is expensive, it's tied to one embodiment, one lab, one set of objects. You end up with datasets that are tiny and narrow compared to what a foundation model needs. Humans, on the other hand, are constantly generating manipulation behavior. We cook, we fold laundry, we assemble furniture, we fumble with keys. If you put a camera on someone's head, or just mine the egocentric video that already exists, you get an enormous amount of data about how objects are approached, grasped, reoriented, how tasks decompose into steps, what recovery looks like when something slips.

What that data is really good for, in my view, is the "what" and the "how" at a semantic and spatial level. What are the subgoals of making a sandwich? Where do hands go relative to a jar lid? What does a reasonable trajectory for pouring look like? Those priors transfer surprisingly well, because the structure of the task is about the world and the objects, not about whether you have five fingers or a two-finger gripper.

Where it falls short is the low-level control. Human hands are incredibly capable and the dynamics of a robot are different, so you can't just copy joint angles. The way I think about it is that human data gives you a very strong prior, and then you need a comparatively small amount of robot data, or simulation, or RL, to ground that prior in the specific body you have. That's a much better division of labor than trying to teleoperate your way to a billion robot episodes.

The other thing people underestimate is that human data encodes intent. When you watch someone do a task, you see not just motions but choices, like which object they pick up first, when they pause to check something. That's the kind of signal that's really hard to get from scripted or random robot data, and it's exactly what you need if you want robots operating in homes rather than in cages on a factory floor.

So, will it alone make a human-level robot? No. But I think any path to that goal that ignores it is going to be much slower, because you'd be throwing away the largest source of manipulation experience on the planet.

r001.rationale: The response compares language and vision breakthroughs powered by billions of human-produced internet examples with robotics’ potential to use human manipulation demonstrations as scalable training data.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that human activity contains a lot of the knowledge we want robots to have. When you watch someone make coffee, you see more than a hand moving through space. You see which objects matter, how the steps fit together, and how the person responds when something doesn’t work. First-person video gives us a rich view of that interaction, and humans can collect it while doing everyday tasks.

But I wouldn’t say that simply watching enough human video gives you a human-level robot. There’s a gap between understanding what a person is doing and knowing how to do it with a robot’s body. The hands are different, the available motions are different, and video doesn’t directly tell you the forces or contact conditions.

So the opportunity is to learn broadly from human data, then use robot experience to ground that knowledge in physical actions. Human data can provide the breadth—what tasks look like and how people approach them—while robot data teaches the system what it can actually execute. That combination is what makes this direction promising to me.

r001.rationale: The response says human activity data can help robots learn tasks, but it does not compare this to human data enabling LLMs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that human activity contains a lot of information about how to interact with the physical world. When you watch someone make coffee, you see more than a sequence of motions. You see which objects matter, how actions are ordered, and how the person responds when something doesn’t go as expected. First-person data gives us a particularly useful perspective because it connects what someone sees with what their hands are doing.

Collecting that experience directly on robots is difficult to scale. Humans already perform an enormous variety of tasks in different environments, so learning from that experience could give robots a much broader foundation.

But there’s still a gap between observing a human and controlling a robot. A robot has a different body, and video alone doesn’t tell you everything about contact or force. So I see human data as a way to learn useful representations and behaviors, with robot interaction providing the feedback needed to ground those behaviors in the robot’s own capabilities. That combination is what makes the direction exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says human experience can provide robots with a broad foundation, but it does not compare this to human data enabling LLMs.
